title: Aggression Across Time
premise: A source-conscious historical survey of human aggressiveness across eras and regions, examining how violence has been shaped by social organization, material conditions, political authority, technology, cultural norms, and individual behavior. The book distinguishes aggression from warfare, coercion, punishment, exploitation, and structural harm while acknowledging that historical evidence is uneven and that no single cause explains every episode.
audience: General readers curious about history, human behavior, and the changing forms of conflict.

chapters.title: Naming the Human Problem
chapters.summary: Defines aggression as a historical object of study and separates interpersonal harm, warfare, coercion, punishment, exploitation, and structural violence. Establishes why records of violence are uneven and why apparent changes across time require careful comparison.
keyBeats: Introduce the distinction between aggressive behavior, organized warfare, and institutional coercion.
Explain how chronicles, laws, burials, art, administrative records, and demographic evidence reveal different aspects of violence.
Set out the book's central dimensions: motive, organization, target, scale, legitimacy, and technology.
Introduce the problem of silence in historical sources, including the under-recording of domestic and marginalized people's experiences.

chapters.title: Small Groups, Kinship, and the First Boundaries
chapters.summary: Examines how mobile communities and early settled societies could combine cooperation within a group with suspicion or violence across group boundaries. The chapter presents environmental pressure, kinship obligations, reputation, and retaliation as interacting conditions rather than universal causes.
keyBeats: Introduce evidence used to discuss interpersonal violence and conflict before extensive written records.
Explain how kinship can provide protection while also extending obligations of revenge.
Examine the effects of settlement, storage, seasonal scarcity, and competition over access to land or water.
Introduce the role of ritual, display, and reputation in making aggression meaningful to a group.
Show why evidence from one archaeological region cannot stand for all early societies.

chapters.title: Cities, Laws, and Authorized Force
chapters.summary: Explores the emergence of cities and states as systems that could suppress some private violence while authorizing punishment, war, and unequal control. Laws are read as evidence of anxieties and institutions, not as direct measurements of everyday behavior.
keyBeats: Introduce the city as a setting where strangers, property, status, and authority require formal regulation.
Read selected legal provisions as evidence of ranked penalties, bodily harm, debt, family control, and state enforcement.
Explain how centralized authority can limit vendetta while expanding the scale of organized coercion.
Distinguish the existence of a law from proof that the prohibited behavior was common.

chapters.title: Rome and the Business of Conquest
chapters.summary: Narrates a single extended case: Rome's expansion from a regional power into an imperial state. The chapter follows how military organization, political competition, taxation, enslavement, citizenship, geography, and material rewards interacted across one historical trajectory without treating Roman expansion as a model for all empires.
keyBeats: Introduce Rome's early military and political setting as a bounded case rather than a universal stage of development.
Trace how elite competition and public honors could reward military success.
Follow the transformation of conquest into land, revenue, captives, administrative control, and new political claims.
Examine how Roman citizenship and provincial governance combined inclusion, hierarchy, and force.
Show how resistance, negotiation, local alliances, and imperial retaliation shaped the case.
Assess the limits of literary sources that celebrate victory and understate the experience of conquered populations.

chapters.title: Honor, Faith, and the Legitimate Blow
chapters.summary: Studies the cultural systems that define when aggression is honorable, shameful, sacred, or criminal. It compares selected historical settings without assuming that honor cultures, religious belief, or patriarchy operate identically across regions.
keyBeats: Introduce honor as a social relationship involving reputation, rank, insult, and public recognition.
Examine how religious language can condemn violence, authorize it, or place conditions on its use.
Analyze gendered expectations surrounding protection, obedience, dominance, and retaliation.
Show how communities distinguish permitted force from illegitimate cruelty.
Introduce the problem of reading ideals and prescriptions as evidence of actual conduct.

chapters.title: Hunger, Wealth, and Unequal Risk
chapters.summary: Investigates the material conditions associated with conflict, including resource competition, poverty, trade, extraction, slavery, and economic inequality. It emphasizes that scarcity and wealth do not mechanically produce violence; institutions and political choices shape their effects.
keyBeats: Introduce the difference between material stress, economic motive, and political mobilization.
Examine how land, food, labor, trade routes, and taxable wealth can become objects of conflict.
Distinguish evidence linking poverty or commodity dependence to conflict from claims about inequality alone.
Show how elites and institutions distribute the risks and rewards of aggression unevenly.

chapters.title: Weapons, Distance, and the Organization of Harm
chapters.summary: Traces how military technologies alter the organization, range, speed, and visibility of aggression from early weapons through gunpowder, industrial warfare, and remote systems. Technology is treated as a force that changes possibilities while remaining dependent on logistics, institutions, and decisions.
keyBeats: Introduce the relationship between weapons, training, supply, fortification, and political organization.
Examine how gunpowder changed siege warfare, battlefield risk, and the balance between armor and firearms.
Trace the industrial transformation of production, transport, artillery, and mass mobilization.
Explain how mechanization and air power increased distance between decision-makers and victims.
Introduce cyber and informational operations as forms of pressure whose harms and boundaries require careful definition.

chapters.title: States, Nations, and Mass Mobilization
chapters.summary: Explores the modern state's capacity to classify populations, mobilize citizens, police borders, and organize violence at unprecedented scale. The chapter focuses on institutions and political narratives rather than presenting modernity as a simple rise or fall in aggression.
keyBeats: Introduce bureaucracy, censuses, passports, taxation, and conscription as tools that can organize both protection and exclusion.
Examine nationalism and the construction of enemies through education, propaganda, and public ceremony.
Show how industrial administration connects factories, railways, armies, prisons, and civilian populations.
Distinguish battlefield violence, state terror, ethnic persecution, and genocide as related but analytically distinct forms.
Explain why official records can be simultaneously abundant and deliberately deceptive.

chapters.title: A Law Read Closely: The Code of Hammurabi
chapters.summary: Reads a single surviving legal document as a compact historical object. The chapter moves through its prologue, selected provisions, penalties, social distinctions, and royal claims while explaining what the text can and cannot establish about everyday violence in ancient Babylonia.
keyBeats: Introduce the document's material and political setting without treating its prologue as a neutral description.
Read selected provisions concerning bodily injury, property, household authority, labor, and status.
Examine how graduated penalties encode social hierarchy.
Close by identifying the limits of using one legal text to reconstruct ordinary behavior.

chapters.title: Bodies, Brains, and Learned Aggression
chapters.summary: Brings historical interpretation into dialogue with research on biology, development, cognition, social learning, and environmental stress. It presents these factors as interacting possibilities and avoids converting population-level associations into predictions about individuals or societies.
keyBeats: Introduce the distinction between reactive aggression and planned or instrumental aggression.
Explain how brain systems, hormones, development, and inherited variation may influence behavior without determining it.
Examine social learning, hostile interpretations, trauma, and exposure to violence as developmental influences.
Discuss heat, crowding, noise, alcohol, and deprivation as conditional stressors rather than universal triggers.
Clarify why findings about contemporary behavior cannot be transferred directly to distant historical populations.
Set explicit boundaries around what behavioral research can contribute to historical explanation.

chapters.title: When Order Breaks
chapters.summary: Examines civil conflict, state failure, occupation, displacement, and the breakdown of ordinary restraints. The chapter focuses on how institutions, identities, fear, opportunity, and retaliation can interact when authority becomes contested.
keyBeats: Introduce the difference between weak institutions, contested sovereignty, and total administrative collapse.
Show how rumors, insecurity, armed groups, and forced movement alter calculations of risk.
Examine how group histories and dehumanizing categories can make aggression appear defensive or necessary.
Trace how ordinary officials, neighbors, soldiers, and opportunists can occupy different roles within the same conflict.
Discuss why post-conflict testimony and official archives may disagree about responsibility and sequence.
Introduce the long afterlife of displacement, trauma, property loss, and remembered grievance.

chapters.title: What History Can and Cannot Explain
chapters.summary: Synthesizes the survey's findings without claiming a single law of human aggression. It compares the explanatory reach of biology, environment, economy, culture, political institutions, and technology, then closes with a bounded account of how historical conditions make some forms of harm more likely and others less legitimate or less available.
keyBeats: Synthesize the recurring interaction between human capacities, institutions, material conditions, identities, and decisions.
Clarify why changes in recorded violence may reflect changes in behavior, recording, population, state power, or all four.
Compare the different meanings of aggression across interpersonal, domestic, imperial, economic, informational, and military settings.
State what the historical record supports about variation, continuity, and uncertainty.
End with a measured account of responsibility that preserves human agency without denying structural constraint.

promises: The book will define the central terms before using them comparatively.
The book will follow one extended historical case in depth rather than presenting only disconnected examples.
The book will read one historical legal document closely and show both its value and its limits.
The book will connect historical evidence with behavioral and social research without treating either field as sufficient on its own.
The book will explain how institutions can restrain some forms of aggression while organizing others.
The conclusion will offer a bounded account of what historical comparison can explain and where uncertainty remains.

openingHook: A settlement on the edge of a changing landscape becomes the first question: when people fight over food, status, land, or fear, which part of the conflict belongs to human impulses, and which part belongs to the world they have built?

authorStance.thesis: Human aggressiveness has appeared in many historical forms, but its scale, targets, legitimacy, and consequences have been repeatedly shaped by institutions, resources, social norms, political incentives, and available technologies.
refusals: The author refuses to explain every historical conflict with one biological, economic, or cultural cause.
The author refuses to treat casualty counts as a complete measure of human aggressiveness.
The author refuses to turn disputed evidence into confident historical fact.
The author refuses to end chapters with a vague claim that history simply repeats itself.
positions: Aggression is a broad category that includes more than battlefield violence.
Historical societies have often regulated aggression within groups while directing it toward outsiders.
States can restrain interpersonal violence and organize violence on a larger scale at the same time.
Material pressure matters, but it becomes violent through institutions, identities, decisions, and expectations.
Modern technology changes the reach and distance of aggression without removing older motives such as fear, status, profit, and belonging.
authorStance.voiceSample:
In 1914, a railway timetable could carry a government decision from Berlin to a frontier faster than a cavalry officer once crossed a province. The printed page looked administrative: columns, stations, departures, arrivals. Alongside it stood the practical problem of moving men, horses, rifles, food, and medical supplies toward a border whose villages had their own names and harvests.

At Verdun in 1916, steel arrived in quantities that altered the meaning of shelter. A concrete wall, a trench corner, or a fold in the ground could decide whether a body remained visible after the next barrage. The artillery crews often saw no individual opponent. Their work passed through maps, coordinates, clocks, and orders before it reached the field.

In 1945, the photograph of a mushroom cloud over Hiroshima compressed several kinds of distance into one image. The aircraft was far above the city. The people below could not see the men who had selected the target. The document that followed was a report, while the burned streets supplied evidence of a different kind. Between those objects stood a chain of laboratories, factories, commanders, and political choices.

illustrationPlan.coverPrompt: A restrained historical collage showing a weathered legal tablet, a city wall, a road leading toward an industrial skyline, and a small map-like network of routes. No text, no author name, no sensational gore, and no single era presented as the whole of human history.
illustrationPlan.globalStyle: Restrained documentary history: maps, artifacts, documents, built environments, tools, and clearly labeled historical scenes. Use muted natural colors, readable composition, and no invented spectacle.
